Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general

Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over.
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Helicopter): Helicopter or aircraft sounds
issues.explanation: The trigger set is strongly combat/assault-themed (helicopters, being followed, people in uniform) and is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. A clinician would question whether these triggers belong to a different trauma history.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: The threat items similarly suggest interpersonal attack or pursuit/hypervigilance in dangerous public settings (checking locks, needing back to wall) rather than a coherent threat representation linked to a child's medical crisis. Given the very strong Triggers → Threat edge, these threat items should plausibly arise from the listed triggers, but both sets point to a different trauma context than the indexed illness trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: The profile centers on a child's life-threatening illness, but 'being followed or tracked' suggests a stalking/pursuit trauma context that is hard to reconcile with the trauma type and the other selected medical-trauma items.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The threat items emphasize interpersonal attack/intrusion vigilance (door-lock checking, needing back to wall) rather than danger linked to medical crisis, loss, or recurrence of illness. In combination with the stalking-like trigger, this pulls the profile toward a persecution/assault formulation that is not clinically coherent with the stated trauma.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Figures: People in uniform
issues.explanation: For trauma centred on a child's life-threatening illness, 'people in uniform' is a poor fit as a trigger unless the trauma involved military or police contexts; it does not cohere well with the otherwise medical/illness-based profile.

issues.item: Threat: Back to Wall: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
issues.explanation: 'Back to wall' implies a hypervigilant interpersonal/assault-style danger schema about monitoring the room, which is hard to reconcile with the illness/medical trauma profile and the other listed triggers and memory items that centre on medical procedures and intrusive reliving.

vignette: Mr. Tran was a widowed 75-year-old South Eastern Asian male who worked as a cybersecurity analyst. His life took a harrowing turn when his young child fell critically ill several years ago. The traumatic event of watching his child fight for their life in the hospital left an indelible mark on Mr. Tran’s psyche, and he now sought help to navigate through the distressing aftermath. The trauma was so vivid that even the slightest reminder could send him spiraling back into the depths of fear and horror. One day at work, while reading a report filled with clinical terms, he caught a whiff of antiseptic from a colleague who had recently been to the hospital. The smell instantly transported Mr. Tran back to the sterile environment where his child lay in critical condition. This olfactory trigger was potent because it was tied directly to the stark and terrifying moments he experienced there. Mr. Tran found that undergoing any medical examination or procedure could elicit a visceral reaction within him. Every time he had to visit a doctor, the fear of reliving those harrowing days would grip him tightly, making his heart race and his hands shake uncontrollably. The memory felt not just like a film but like something happening right now—his body reacting as if the stressful experience were actually unfolding again before his eyes. The recurrence of these triggers heightened Mr. Tran’s sense of threat. He was certain that any reminder of those days would unleash the same overwhelming negative emotions he had experienced during his child's illness. This fear made it difficult for him to seek medical care, even when necessary. For example, despite having chronic pain issues, he avoided going to doctors out of sheer dread. Mr. Tran’s memories were like a film that played over and over again in his mind. He would often find himself reliving the moments of panic and despair, unable to break free from the loop. These vivid recollections made it almost impossible for him to distinguish between past and present. When he tried to explain what had happened, he would get lost in the details, losing the thread of his narrative mid-sentence. The fear and physical reactivity associated with these triggers further reinforced his negative appraisals about the traumatic event itself. The memory of watching helplessly as his child battled for their life made every subsequent encounter with medical reminders a potent threat. This cycle tightened over time: each trigger reignited the memory, which in turn heightened his sense of threat and physical reactivity. One day, while at work, Mr. Tran received an email from a colleague about a new case involving hospital security breaches. The mention of hospitals and medical procedures immediately triggered a flashback, and he felt as if he were back in that sterile room with his child fighting for life. His hands trembled uncontrollably, and he could feel the panic rising within him. He realized then that these experiences were taking an immense toll on both his personal well-being and his professional capabilities. Mr. Tran had come to believe that avoiding any potential trigger was the only way to manage his distress, but this avoidance strategy had significant consequences. His work performance suffered as he found it increasingly difficult to focus amidst constant reminders of the hospital environment. He knew deep down that there must be a better way to cope with these memories and triggers. Ultimately, what finally brought Mr. Tran to seek help was a profound realization: he could no longer bear living in perpetual fear of reliving those harrowing days. His greatest hope was to regain control over his life and find ways to process the trauma without it dictating every aspect of his existence.
